steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on Trojan Playground, a reinforcement learning framework for hardware Trojan insertion and detection. Explain the supply-chain threat, the weaknesses of current HT benchmarks and detectors, our RL-based tools, the threat model, our contributions and results, and the paper outline.

steps.text:

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Threat background
  - DoD report, 2022: 88% of production and 98% of assembly, packaging, testing of chips done outside US
  - multi-party production -> concerns about malicious modifications = Hardware Trojan (HT) insertion
  - HT = any design/manufacturing violation in an IC concerning its intent; on activation -> erroneous outputs (Figure 1), possibly information leak
  - adversarial model of Shakya et al.: insertion scenarios
    - compromised employees infect design source code or netlist
    - third-party IPs (processing cores, memory modules, I/O components, network-on-chip) bought to cut time-to-market and cost; untrusted vendors = risk
    - untrusted foundry reverse-engineers GDSII layout to get netlist, inserts HTs
    - malicious third-party CAD tools insert HTs
- Problems
  - researchers mostly use benchmarks of Shakya et al. and Salmani et al.; many detection approaches built on them over past decade
  - benchmarks limited in size and variety -> hard to train ML HT detectors; leave-one-out cross-validation helps but doesn't solve it
  - human bias in insertion phase (designer's mindset); e.g. some benchmarks only consider signal activity, HTs randomly inserted into pool of rare nets
  - flawed insertion -> detectors tuned to flawed scenarios; adversaries combine ideas, detectors fall short
  - almost no HT detectors publicly available -> latency for newcomers
- Our tools
  - RL-based HT insertion: creates new benchmarks per user criteria; criteria = user-modified RL rewarding function; netlist = environment; agent maximizes reward; tunable rewarding scheme
  - prepares community for HTs inserted by non-human (AI) agents
  - RL-based HT detector, tunable rewarding function; three detection rewarding functions studied
  - agent finds test vectors with highest reward; vectors activate HTs; test engineer applies them and checks output vs golden model
- Unified framework
  - users only set parameters, no human intervention
  - previous automation efforts need intermediate effort -> can't create vast quantity of HTs (Section II)
- Threat model
  - like previous work: perpetrator can insert HTs into netlist; netlist via reverse-engineering in foundry; triggers built and placed in layout
  - defense: security engineer gets post-silicon hard IP, maybe with HTs; uses golden model to generate minimal test vectors activating as many HTs as possible
  - doesn't know insertion criteria; vectors based on multiple insertion mentalities; output deviation -> malicious behavior
- Contributions (vs our previous publications)
  - tunable RL-based HT insertion tool, free of human bias, large population of valid HTs per design
  - tunable RL-based multi-criteria HT detection tool
  - generic methodology to compare HT detectors fairly; confidence value metric
- Results: average 90.54% detection rate on our HT-inserted benchmarks; compared with state of the art; finds previously unidentifiable HTs
- Organization: II related work + RL fundamentals; III insertion; IV detection; V comparison methodology; VI results; VII conclusion

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
According to a DoD report released in 2022, 88\% of the production and 98\% of the assembly, packaging and testing of microelectronic chips are done outside of the US. This growing multi-party production model has raised a lot of security concerns about malicious modifications in the design and fabrication of chips, which is called Hardware Trojan (HT) insertion. HTs are defined as any design or manufacturing violations in an integrated circuit (IC) with respect to the intent of the IC. When an HT is activated, it can cause erroneous outputs (e.g., Figure 1) and maybe leak information. In the adversarial model introduced by Shakya et al., HTs can be inserted into target ICs in the following scenarios:

- Compromised employees can infect the design source code or netlist with HTs.

- Third-party intellectual properties (IPs) such as processing cores, memory modules, I/O components and network-on-chip are often bought and put into a design to speed up time-to-market and lower design costs. But integrating IPs from untrusted vendors can be a risk to the security and integrity of the IC.

- An untrusted foundry can reverse-engineer the GDSII physical layout to get the netlist and insert HTs into it.

- Malicious third-party CAD tools can also insert HTs into designs.

Researchers have mostly used the established benchmarks reported by Shakya et al. and Salmani et al. as a reference to study the impact of HTs. Many HT detection approaches have been developed based on these benchmarks over the past decade. These benchmarks were a valuable effort for the community, but they are limited in the size and variety that is needed to push detection tools into more realistic modern scenarios. For example, the small set of benchmarks makes it hard to use and train machine learning (ML) HT detectors, where more training data negatively impacts classification accuracy. Some studies tried to alleviate this by shuffling data for ML-based detectors, e.g., the leave-one-out cross-validation method, but this does not solve the problem entirely. The existing HT benchmarks also have an inherent human bias in the insertion phase, because they are tightly coupled with the designer's mindset. For example, some of the HT benchmarks only consider signal activity for HT insertion, i.e., the HTs are randomly inserted into a pool of available rare nets of the circuit. These flaws in the insertion phase simplify the complexity of the problem, and security researchers end up developing HT detectors that are finely tuned to flawed scenarios. Adversaries, on the other hand, come up with new HT attacks that combine different ideas, and the detectors fall short of exposing them. Another problem, which is equally important, is that almost no HT detectors are publicly available. So other researchers cannot access these tools, and newcomers to hardware security face a considerable latency.

- RL-based HT insertion tool: user criteria = RL rewarding function; netlist is the environment; agent maximizes reward; tunable; prepares for HTs from AI agents
- RL-based HT detector with tunable reward; three detection rewarding functions; agent finds highest-reward test vectors; test engineer compares output to golden model
- Unified framework: only parameters, no human intervention; previous automation needs intermediate effort, so no vast quantity of HTs (Section II)
- Threat model: perpetrator inserts HTs into netlist (reverse-engineered in foundry); security engineer with post-silicon hard IP + golden model generates minimal test vectors; doesn't know insertion criteria; deviation -> malicious behavior
- Contributions vs our previous publications: tunable insertion tool free of human bias; multi-criteria detection tool; fair comparison methodology with confidence value metric
- Results: average 90.54 % detection rate; finds previously unidentifiable HTs
- Organization: Sections II-VII

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
According to a DoD report released in 2022, 88\% of the production and 98\% of the assembly, packaging and testing of microelectronic chips are done outside of the US. This growing multi-party production model has raised a lot of security concerns about malicious modifications in the design and fabrication of chips, which is called Hardware Trojan (HT) insertion. HTs are defined as any design or manufacturing violations in an integrated circuit (IC) with respect to the intent of the IC. When an HT is activated, it can cause erroneous outputs (e.g., Figure 1) and maybe leak information. In the adversarial model introduced by Shakya et al., HTs can be inserted into target ICs in the following scenarios:

- Compromised employees can infect the design source code or netlist with HTs.

- Third-party intellectual properties (IPs) such as processing cores, memory modules, I/O components and network-on-chip are often bought and put into a design to speed up time-to-market and lower design costs. But integrating IPs from untrusted vendors can be a risk to the security and integrity of the IC.

- An untrusted foundry can reverse-engineer the GDSII physical layout to get the netlist and insert HTs into it.

- Malicious third-party CAD tools can also insert HTs into designs.

Researchers have mostly used the established benchmarks reported by Shakya et al. and Salmani et al. as a reference to study the impact of HTs. Many HT detection approaches have been developed based on these benchmarks over the past decade. These benchmarks were a valuable effort for the community, but they are limited in the size and variety that is needed to push detection tools into more realistic modern scenarios. For example, the small set of benchmarks makes it hard to use and train machine learning (ML) HT detectors, where more training data negatively impacts classification accuracy. Some studies tried to alleviate this by shuffling data for ML-based detectors, e.g., the leave-one-out cross-validation method, but this does not solve the problem entirely. The existing HT benchmarks also have an inherent human bias in the insertion phase, because they are tightly coupled with the designer's mindset. For example, some of the HT benchmarks only consider signal activity for HT insertion, i.e., the HTs are randomly inserted into a pool of available rare nets of the circuit. These flaws in the insertion phase simplify the complexity of the problem, and security researchers end up developing HT detectors that are finely tuned to flawed scenarios. Adversaries, on the other hand, come up with new HT attacks that combine different ideas, and the detectors fall short of exposing them. Another problem, which is equally important, is that almost no HT detectors are publicly available. So other researchers cannot access these tools, and newcomers to hardware security face a considerable latency.

This work tries to move this research space forward by developing next-generation HT insertion and detection methods based on reinforcement learning. Our RL-based HT insertion tool creates new HT benchmarks according to criteria the user gives to the tool. The insertion criteria is an RL rewarding function modified by the user, and the RL agent then inserts HTs into designs automatically. The netlist is the environment, and the RL agent tries to insert HTs in it to maximize the reward it gets. The rewarding scheme of the insertion tool is tunable, so it can push the agent toward a specific goal in the training session. Our insertion tool is a step towards preparing the community for future HTs inserted by non-human agents, e.g., AI agents. We also propose an RL-based HT detector with a tunable rewarding function, which helps detect inserted HTs based on different strategies. We studied three different detection rewarding functions for the RL detector agent. The agent finds the test vectors that give the highest reward for each reward function. These test vectors then activate and find HTs in the IC. The test engineer applies the test vectors to the chip and monitors the output for deviations from the golden model.

Our toolset lets researchers do HT insertion and detection in one unified framework. Users only need to set the parameters to insert and detect HTs, without human intervention. There were previous efforts to automate HT insertion and detection, but they need an intermediate effort, which stops us from creating a vast quantity of HTs (more explanation in Section II).

Like several previous works, our threat model assumes that the perpetrator can insert HTs into the netlist of a design. The netlist can be obtained in the foundry with state-of-the-art reverse-engineering techniques, and the HT triggers are constructed and placed in the design layout. On the defense side, we assume a security engineer gets a post-silicon hard IP that may or may not contain malicious HTs. The security engineer uses a golden model to generate a set of minimal test vectors to activate as many HTs as possible. The test engineer does not know the insertion criteria, but they generate test vectors based on multiple insertion mentalities. If the output(s) of the design-under-test deviate(s) from the golden model, this can point to malicious behavior.

Compared with our previous publications, we make the following contributions in this paper:

- We developed a tunable RL-based HT insertion tool that is free of human bias and can insert HTs automatically and create a large population of valid HTs for each design.

- We introduce a tunable RL-based multi-criteria HT detection tool that helps a security engineer be better prepared for different HT insertion strategies.

- We introduce and use a generic methodology to compare HT detectors fairly. It is based on the confidence value metric, which helps the security engineer choose the right detector based on the application and security requirements of the chip.

Our results show that our detection tool, with all three detection approaches, has an average 90.54 % detection rate on our HT-inserted benchmarks. We compare these results to existing state-of-the-art detection methods and show how our techniques find HTs that could not be identified before. We believe HT detection will be implemented as a variety of detection strategies, so the uniquely identified HTs suggest that our detection techniques and framework are important contributions to this space.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows: Section II reviews related work and explains the fundamentals of RL. Sections III and IV present how our HT insertion and detection approaches work. Section V introduces our HT comparison methodology. Section VI shows the experimental results, and Section VII concludes the paper.

This work attempts to move this research space forward by developing next-generation HT insertion and detection methods based on reinforcement learning. The RL-based HT insertion tool creates new HT benchmarks according to the criteria passed to the tool by the user. The insertion criteria is an RL rewarding function modified by the user, and the RL agent then inserts HTs into designs automatically. The netlist is considered an environment in which the RL agent tries to insert HTs to maximize the gained reward. The rewarding scheme of the insertion tool is tunable, which can push the agent toward a specific goal in the training session. Our insertion tool is a step towards preparing the community for future HTs inserted by non-human agents, e.g., AI agents. We also propose an RL-based HT detector with a tunable rewarding function that helps detect inserted HTs based on various strategies. To explore this space, we studied three different detection rewarding functions for the RL detector agent. The agent finds the test vectors yielding the highest rewards for each reward function, and the generated test vectors then activate and find HTs in the IC. The test engineer passes the test vectors to the chip and monitors the output for deviations from the golden model.

Our proposed toolset enables researchers to experience HT insertion and detection within a unified framework, which only requires users to set the parameters to insert and detect HTs without human intervention. There have been previous efforts to automate the HT insertion and detection process [13,11,14]; however, they need an intermediate effort that hinders us from creating a vast quantity of HTs (more explanation in Section II).

Similar to several previous works [10,15,2,16,17], this paper's threat model assumes that the perpetrator is capable of inserting HTs into a design's netlist. The netlist can be obtained through state-of-the-art reverse-engineering techniques in the foundry, and HT triggers are constructed and placed in the design layout. On the defense side, we assume a security engineer receives a post-silicon hard IP that may or may not contain malicious HTs. Using a golden model, the security engineer generates a set of minimal test vectors to activate as many HTs as possible. The test engineer does not know the insertion criteria; however, they generate test vectors based on multiple insertion mentalities. If the output(s) of the design-under-test deviate(s) from the golden model, it can indicate malicious behavior.

We make the following contributions in this paper with respect to our previous publications [18,19]:

- • We developed a tunable RL-based HT insertion tool free of human bias, capable of automatic HT insertion and of creating a large population of valid HTs for each design.

- • We introduce a tunable RL-based multi-criteria HT detection tool that helps a security engineer better prepare for different HT insertion strategies.

- • We introduce and use a generic methodology to compare HT detectors fairly. The methodology is based on the confidence value metric, which helps the security engineer select the proper detector based on the chip's application and security requirements.

Our results show that our detection tool with all three detection approaches has an average 90.54 % detection rate for our HT-inserted benchmarks. We compare these detection results to existing state-of-the-art detection methods and show how our techniques find previously unidentifiable HTs. As we believe that HT detection will be implemented as a variety of detection strategies, the uniquely identified HTs suggest that our detection techniques and framework are important contributions to this space.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section II reviews the related work and explains the fundamentals of RL. Sections III and IV present the mechanics of our proposed HT insertion and detection approaches, respectively. Section V introduces our HT comparison methodology. Section VI demonstrates the experimental results, and Section VII concludes the paper.
